newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson merchandise dead as Nicole Brown.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson merchandise dead as Nicole Brown.

text.p: If O.J. Simpson is looking to raise money selling his autograph and other memorabilia to pay damages from the civil trial, perhaps he should think again.
In the months before and after the criminal trial in October 1995, when a jury acquitted Simpson of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, prices for all things O.J. were on the rise.

But the finding in the civil trial this month has all but killed the market for O.J. memorabilia, collectors and sports marketing experts said. The jurors blamed Simpson for the 1994 slayings and ordered him to pay $33.5 million in damages.
"I would hate to have an O.J. signature right now," collectibles expert Harry Rinker said.
"It's going to be a long, long time before this man is forgiven," said Roberto Muller, a sports marketing executive who worked with Simpson in the 1970s and has been in the business for 30 years.
All of which indicates that prices for football cards, signed pictures and O.J. dolls, which have fallen steeply, are unlikely to recover any time soon.

"I don't think people want his autograph, or to see his picture in their homes anymore," said Muller, a former Reebok executive whose Muller Sports Group Inc. consults on sports marketing, licensing and other issues.

To be sure, the former football star, sportscaster and advertising pitchman was never as hot a property as current stars like Michael Jordan or older heroes such as Babe Ruth. But Simpson merchhandise had appreciated over the years. O.J. cards reached $50 to $200 apiece, depending on rarity and condition, and the dolls and other items had risen as well.
In fact, the notoriety of the case initially gave Simpson memorabilia a boost, and his Oct. 3, 1995, acquittal on two murder counts also helped.
But the finding in the civil trial and the media's steady 32-month drumbeat about the case has accelerated a decline in prices that started last year, the experts said.
"After the killings, things went up quickly, doubling and tripling in price. But those prices have tumbled," said Rinker.
"O.J. football cards? I understand there's zip demand," said John Koenig, editor of Toy Trader and Discoveries, two magazines for toy and rock music memorabilia collectors.
Accordingly, prices have dropped. Simpson's rookie card, once worth $200, is now at $100 or so, according to Rocky Landsverk at Sports Collectors Digest magazine.
About 1,800 signed O.J. cards sold at auction not long ago in a sports card company bankruptcy. The price? $4 apiece.
Signed photographs have fallen 50 percent or more.
"The whole case just kind of sickened everybody," said Greg Ambrosius, editor of Sports Cards magazine.
Expert testimony in the civil trial, that Simpson could earn as much as $3 million a year from his name, may or may not have been true then but seems dubious now, officials said.
"The fact is, in terms of sponsorship, there is no way, no how that he can really re-establish himself in the corporate world," said Muller.
And his memorabilia will probably have strictly limited appeal -- for a "fanatic" O.J. collector or for someone with "a very dark sense of humour," Muller said.
Despite the drop, rare items such as a jersey worn in his first game or his rookie card may yet prove valuable, experts said. Simpson himself does not control many of these items.
"Some of the older stuff will return to 1992 or '93 prices and may well go up, ultimately," said Rinker. "But I don't think we're going to see too many O.J. fan clubs from here on in."
